trend_impulse_follow.one_line: No bug, no look-ahead and no cost problem was found, but the +24.8% is not evidence of an edge: random entries with the same exposure score the same (real result at the 51st percentile), half of it comes from the Guardian halt rather than the specified rules, it is negative without its best five days, and the Coinbase-only walk-forward makes +3.7% with a -25% drawdown and fails the fees-doubled gate.
implementation_differences: Entry signal: none. A plain-loop re-implementation written from the specification text (own Wilder ATR recursion, own 168-bar volume mean, own 336-bar trend) matched the module on all 40 symbols for 3 grid cells: 3,321,720 rows, 16,567 signals, 0 side differences, 0 stop differences. No limit, take-profit, trail or exit intents are emitted; 0 signals on missing bars; 0 signals with a NaN stop.

What was audited is not only what was specified. The spec's exits are 'time stop after 72 bars or the protective stop'. In the audited validation run 77 of 268 trades (29%) were closed by the engine's Guardian (halt after 3 losing trades in a row, all positions closed at the next open) and those trades carry +$1,927 of the +$2,483. With the Guardian off (the strategy as written) the same walk-forward makes +12.2%, drawdown -16.9%, p = 0.30.

The Guardian effect changes sign between windows: the Hunter's design notes say it cost profit (+77% with it, +119% without); in validation it doubles profit (+24.8% with, +12.2% without). Removing only the 3-losses rule and keeping the daily -3% limit gives +16.9%.

L = 336 is in params but not in the grid, as specified. Walk-forward used 4 different cells across the 6 validation quarters (13, 10, 0, 0, 10, 5); the fixed default cell gives +25.6% with a -18.6% drawdown.
trend_impulse_follow.lookahead_detail: None found. Inputs at row t are close/open/volume of bar t (known at its close), ATR lagged one bar for the move size, the 168-bar volume mean lagged one bar, and the 336-bar return lagged one bar; the stop uses ATR[t], known at the close. harness.leak_test passed with seeds 1, 7, 42 and 2026 (243 probes each across all 18 cells, 0 mismatches, no forbidden code); the audit's own test (457 probes) and trade replay (311 probes) also passed. The strategy does not read the universe; the engine enforces it. I recomputed the top-10 for 2025-02, 2025-06, 2025-11, 2026-03 and 2026-05 from daily volume of the prior 30 days only and got the listed set 10 of 10 each time (a ranking on the month itself would overlap only 7 to 9 of 10). open[t+1] equals close[t] on 100% of BTC, ETH and SOL bars, so the fill is the signal bar's close plus slippage, as the protocol says. No bar from 2026-05-18 onward was loaded (last bar in memory 2026-05-17 23:00 UTC).
trend_impulse_follow.real_cost_check: Costs are understated but are not what breaks it. Modelled one-way entry slippage averaged 3.3 bps (median 2.8); the actual $10k half-spread was 7.1 bps in the signal bar and 9.2 bps in the fill bar (medians 4.0 and 3.6; 95th percentile 16.4 and 12.7; worst 308 and 439 bps). Actual is 1.2 to 1.4 times the model at the median and 2.2 to 2.9 times on average. Exits: time and Guardian exits are close to the model (3.2 vs 3.2 bps and 4.4 vs 3.5 bps); stops are modelled at 6.9 bps against an actual 6.9 bps in the stop bar. Total slippage over 268 trades: $266 modelled, $398 actual (fill bar), $461 using the worse of the two adjacent bars, $548 if stops also pay double the actual. Re-priced trade by trade: +24.8% becomes +23.5% / +22.9% / +22.0%. Full engine re-run with actual half-spreads: +23.0% (bar itself) or +22.4% (worse of two bars), drawdown -11.6%, p = 0.145. One bar late AND actual costs: +20.7% to +21.4%, drawdown -17.2%, p = 0.21 to 0.22. All modelled costs doubled and one bar late: +13.3%, drawdown -18.7%. Costs matter little because positions are small (median notional $1,375, max $4,053, never capped). Timing is unstable, though: delaying entries 0 / 1 / 2 / 3 bars gives +24.8% / +22.0% / +38.8% / +7.5%. Clustering: 268 entries fall in 148 distinct hours; 29 hours had 3 or more simultaneous entries (47% of all trades), 9 hours had 5 or more, up to 9 at once; peak gross exposure $17,903 (1.79x equity). Coinbase whole-contract sizing is not a problem for BTC and ETH: ideal size was 0.9 to 4.6 BTC contracts and 1.9 to 11.8 ETH contracts, no trade rounds to zero, size error averages 8% (BTC) and 4% (ETH), max 19%, risk per trade becomes $42 to $60, P&L changes by under $10. Contract sizes for other Coinbase coins were not checked.
trend_impulse_follow.concentration: Total +$2,483 over 268 trades. By symbol: ETH +$1,014 (41% of profit, 27 trades), ZEC +$519, BNB +$445, TRUMP +$433, AVAX +$414; 11 of 22 symbols lost (XRP -$290, ADA -$249, PEPE -$226). Without ETH's trades +14.7% (engine re-run with ETH untradable: +12.7%, p = 0.27); without the best two symbols +9.5%; best three +5.0%; engine re-run without ETH and BTC +5.7%, p = 0.37. By quarter: 2025Q2 +$1,196 (48%); without it +12.9%. By month: without the best month +16.9%, best two +9.2%, best three +2.3%. By day: the best five of 109 exit days made $3,615; without them the result is -11.3%, without the best ten -27.6%. One entry day (2026-01-29) made $1,175, 47% of the total. By trade: top 5 trades $2,131, top 10 $3,410; without the top 10 trades (3.7% of trades) -9.3%. Win rate 39.6%, median trade -0.50R, mean +0.19R. Long versus short: 100 longs made +$2,598 (+0.52R each); 168 shorts lost -$115, and -$1,819 with the Guardian off, in a window where the top-10 basket fell 62%. Coinbase: dropping the 35 trades in 9 coins Coinbase does not list leaves +22.6% (engine re-run with the same parameter choices: +25.5%, p = 0.10; with the Guardian off +11.6%, p = 0.30). But the full Coinbase-only audit, where the walk-forward re-chooses parameters on Coinbase coins only, gives +3.7%, drawdown -25.0%, 280 trades, p = 0.46, fees doubled -0.9% (gate fails), all costs doubled -4.7%, the last three quarters -8.9% / -2.8% / -8.2%, shorts -$1,436.
trend_impulse_follow.exposure_check: The strategy does not beat a naive rule with the same exposure. Placebo 1 (same symbol-months, same direction, same stop and 72-bar hold, random entry hour), run through the desk engine with the Guardian on, 150 draws: placebo mean +$2,317 (sd $1,261) against the real +$2,483, which sits at the 51st percentile. Requiring the random hour to agree with the 14-day trend: placebo mean +$1,845, real at the 71st percentile. With the Guardian off (standalone simulator that reproduces the engine's guardian-off P&L to the dollar, $1,223; 400 to 500 draws): placebo mean +$2,576 to +$2,678, real at the 15th to 17th percentile, i.e. worse than random timing. This placebo is generous because matching on the symbol-month uses hindsight. Placebo 2 has no hindsight (same symbol, any tradable hour in the window, side = sign of the 14-day trend): mean +$397, sd $1,422, real at the 70.5th percentile, still not distinguishable. The same test on the earlier walk-forward quarters (2023-10 to 2024-12, 261 trades, +$1,213): 9.5th, 62.5th and 86th percentile. By side in validation: real longs are at the 97th to 99.8th percentile of random longs, real shorts at the 0th to 0.2nd percentile of random shorts (random shorts in the same symbol-months made about +$1,480, the real ones lost $1,819). The rule was specified as symmetric, so keeping only the long side would be a choice made after seeing validation.
trend_impulse_follow.luck: The audit's own cluster-bootstrap p-value is 0.120 (day clusters; 0.091 by week) and it does not survive Holm: the threshold for the best of 15 audited ideas is 0.0033, for 32 drafted 0.0016. My t-statistics on the same trades: 1.18 by exit day (109 days), 1.31 by week (55), 1.55 by month (17). If none of the 15 audited ideas had any edge, the chance that the best one shows p <= 0.12 is 85% (98% across 32). The p-value worsens under every stress: 0.145 with actual costs, 0.21 to 0.22 one bar late with actual costs, 0.27 without ETH, 0.30 with the Guardian off, 0.46 on Coinbase coins with their own walk-forward. What the evidence shows: the code does what the spec says, uses no future data, and made money after costs in 5 of 6 validation quarters and 9 of 11 walk-forward quarters, with all 18 grid cells positive (+0.1% to +55.5%). What it does not show: that the average trade is positive beyond chance, that the entry timing adds anything over random entries in the same coins and direction, or that the short half of the rule works at all.
strongest_evidence_against: Same-exposure placebo: random entry hours in the same symbol-months, direction, stop and hold, through the desk engine with the Guardian on, average +23.2% against the real +24.8% (real at the 51st percentile of 150 draws). With the Guardian off the real strategy is at the 15th to 17th percentile of 400 to 500 draws.

Half the return is the Guardian, not the specified rules: Guardian off +12.2% (p = 0.30, drawdown -16.9%) against +24.8% audited; 77 of 268 trades were closed by the 3-losses halt. In the design window the Hunter found the same halt reduced profit, so the sign of this effect is not stable.
Coinbase-only walk-forward (the version the owner can probably trade): +3.7%, drawdown -25.0%, p = 0.46, fees doubled -0.9% (fails gate 4), all costs doubled -4.7%, last three quarters all negative.
Fat-tail dependence: without the best 5 of 109 exit days the result is -11.3%; without the top 10 of 268 trades -9.3%; one entry day (2026-01-29) is 47% of the profit; ETH is 41%.
The short side, 168 of 268 trades, lost money (-$115; -$1,819 with the Guardian off) in a window where the basket fell 62% and random shorts in the same symbol-months made about +$1,480.
p = 0.120 before any multiple-testing correction, t = 1.18 by day; Holm needs 0.0033. The best of 15 no-edge ideas would look this good 85% of the time.

Small timing changes move the answer by more than the claimed edge: entry delayed 0 / 1 / 2 / 3 bars gives +24.8% / +22.0% / +38.8% / +7.5%; grid cells range from +0.1% to +55.5%; every k = 3.0 cell is below +12%.
strongest_evidence_for: Implementation is exact: 0 differences against an independent re-implementation over 3.3 million rows and 16,567 signals.
No look-ahead: 4 extra leak-test seeds (972 probes) with 0 mismatches, and the monthly universe confirmed as ranked on the prior 30 days.

Costs are not the weak point: actual order-book slippage is 1.5 to 2.1 times the model ($398 to $548 against $266), yet the return only falls to +22.0% to +23.5%, and to +20.7% with entries one bar late as well.
All 18 grid cells were profitable in validation; 5 of 6 validation quarters and 9 of 11 walk-forward quarters were positive; the design window was also positive (+83.6% default).
The long side alone is at the 97th to 99.8th percentile of random longs in validation (but only the 23rd to 80th percentile in the earlier walk-forward quarters, so this is not confirmed elsewhere).

Against a hindsight-free 'follow the 14-day trend at random hours' rule the strategy is above the median in both periods (70.5th percentile in validation, 86th in 2023-10 to 2024-12), though neither is significant.
caveats_for_owner: Nothing is broken in the code, the data timing or the cost model. The refutation is about how weak the evidence is, not about an error.

Do not treat +24.8% as the expected return. The rules as written, without the Guardian's 3-losses halt, made +12.2% with a -16.9% drawdown, and on Coinbase-listed coins with their own walk-forward +3.7% with a -25.0% drawdown.
The result is statistically the same as entering at random hours in the same coins and direction. The impulse signal's timing has not been shown to add anything.
Expect to lose on about 60% of trades (median trade -0.5R) and to depend on a few big winners: five days out of 109 made more than the entire profit.
The short side has not worked out of sample. Dropping it now would be a rule fitted to the validation window, so it would need its own fresh test.

If it is paper traded anyway, the Guardian must behave exactly as in the backtest (halt after 3 losses in a row, close everything, resume automatically the next UTC day). A halt that waits for a human to resume is a different strategy from the one audited.
Up to 9 positions opened in the same hour and gross exposure reached 1.79x equity; these positions win and lose together.

The Coinbase list is today's list applied to history, and I only checked whole-contract rounding for BTC and ETH (fine: at most 19% size error). Coinbase fees and funding differ from Kraken's and were not modelled.
A good holdout result on six months would be about 100 trades; with this payoff shape that cannot confirm or kill the edge on its own.

The placebo that matches symbol-months uses hindsight and is therefore a tough comparison; against the hindsight-free placebo the strategy is above the median (70th and 86th percentile) but still within noise.

cross_weekend_follow_alts.one_line: The code is faithful, causal and its costs are realistic, but the +8.6% is not distinguishable from luck: it is one coin (XRP = 86%), three weekends and two quarters, it loses money exactly where its own thesis says it should win, and it should not be relied on as champion.
implementation_differences: None in the signal. My plain-loop re-implementation from the spec text (own Wilder ATR, own universe lookup) matches the module on side, time, symbol and stop price in all 27 grid cells: 0 differences (306 signals in the default cell, 435 in thr=0/stop 4/n 3, 721 with n_alt=5).
No signal falls on a non-tradable or missing-candle row (0 of 435). The engine reproduces the 129 audited validation trades to the cent ($862.40).

Not a code difference, but a reporting one the owner should know: the spec's DEFAULT parameters (thr 0.5%, stop 5, n 3) made only +2.3% in validation (113 trades, shorts -$438). The +8.6% exists because the walk-forward switched to thr=0 for 4 of the 6 validation quarters (94 of 129 trades, $749 of $862).
The spec says the exit is 'time stop only'; in practice 23 of 129 trades left on the protective stop, 1 on a Guardian halt and 2 at fold boundaries. This is engine behaviour, not a bug.
cross_weekend_follow_alts.lookahead_detail: No look-ahead found. Every input in row t (BTC and alt close at t and t-48, ATR(24) through t) is known at the close of the Sunday 21:00 bar. harness.leak_test passed with 0 mismatches on seeds 1, 7 and 42 (306 probes each, all 27 cells); a fourth seed was still running when I wrote this. The audit's own run had 363 probes plus 112 trade replays, all clean. Universe: I recomputed the top-3 alts for 38 months (2023-04 to 2026-05) from daily volume ranked on the 30 days before each month, reading only rows before VALIDATION_END: 0 mismatches, and no month matches an in-month ranking instead. The strategy indexes the list by the signal bar's own month. One-bar-late is unchanged (+8.64%), so the result does not depend on filling at the signal bar's close.
cross_weekend_follow_alts.real_cost_check: Costs are not the problem. Entry half-spread for $10k: modelled mean 2.65 bps (median 2.14); actual in the two bars around the fill 2.91 (2.22); worst of three bars 3.49. Exits: modelled 3.27, actual 3.90, worst 4.35. Actual exceeded modelled on 63% of entries, largest 11 bps. Total slippage: $88 modelled, $98 actual, $112 worst case. Validation return re-priced: +8.53% with actual costs, +8.38% worst-of-three-bars, against +8.62% modelled. One bar late AND actual costs: +8.57%; with fees doubled as well: +6.95%. Positions are small (median notional $1,088, max $3,383), so the $10k depth figure overstates their cost. All 129 entries are at Sunday 22:00 UTC; 94% enter alongside another position (33 of 52 weekends open three at once); largest gross $7,314 (0.73x equity). Whole-contract sizing on Coinbase (XRP 500, SOL 5, DOGE 5,000, ADA 1,000, SUI 500, LTC 5, ZEC 1 coins, from Coinbase's public product list) does distort: the median wanted size is 1.2 XRP contracts, 1.8 SOL, 1.0 DOGE. On the 127 Coinbase-listed trades ($913 fractional), round-to-nearest skips 13 trades and gives $1,066 with risk of $34-$94 per trade; round-down skips 37 and gives $531; forcing at least one contract gives $768 with risk up to $293 on a single trade. The rounding rule alone moves the result by about +/-$270.
cross_weekend_follow_alts.concentration: Severe. By symbol: XRP $743 of $862 (86%, 44 trades), SOL $216, ZEC $56, LTC $41, SUI $22, WIF -$50, DOGE -$71, ADA -$94. Without XRP: $119 (+1.2%). By quarter: 2025-Q4 $287 and 2026-Q1 $557 are 98% of the profit; the other four quarters sum to +$18 and three of the six are negative. Without the best quarter: $305 (+3.1%). By weekend (52 traded, 28 winners): the best three ($404, $277, $199) exceed the whole profit, leaving -$18; without the best five weekends (the same as the best five exit days): -$330. Top 10 trades made $1,183, the other 119 lost $321. Long versus short: longs 63 trades +$985 (60% winners), shorts 66 trades -$123 (41% winners). Dropping the only non-Coinbase coin (WIF, 2 trades) gives $913. The desk's Coinbase-subset audit (+12.4%, p 0.095) shows the same shape: XRP $855 and SOL $398 against a $1,243 total.
cross_weekend_follow_alts.exposure_check: Three nulls, built with a stand-alone simulator that matches the engine to the cent on time and stop exits (127 of 129 trades, $766 in the simulator). (A) Same symbols, side, stop multiple and 24h hold, entered at a random hour of the same calendar month, one draw per weekend so simultaneous entries stay together, 1,000 draws: mean -$29, 5th-95th percentile -$1,034 to +$1,043; 10.3% of draws do as well as the real $766. That is roughly the 90th percentile, not significant. (B) The identical rule at each of the 168 hour-of-week slots: mean $69, 56% of slots profitable, best $1,735; Sunday 21:00 ranks 35th, so 20.8% of slots do as well or better. Weekend-signal slots average $462 against -$88 for weekday slots, so there is a mild weekend flavour but nothing special about the chosen hour. Engine re-runs with only the signal hour moved: Sun 17:00 $492, 18:00 $81, 19:00 $196, 20:00 $392, [21:00 $862], 22:00 $69, 23:00 $1, Mon 00:00 -$689, 01:00 -$82, 02:00 $20. The spec hour is the best of ten adjacent hours; the median neighbour is $69. (C) Same weekends and symbols with the side chosen by coin flip per weekend, 5,000 draws: mean -$427, 5.6% do as well as the real result. But the same Sunday trades taken always LONG make $685, and always long in all top-3 alts with no BTC signal and no agreement filter makes $872 on 177 trades, more than the strategy; always short makes -$1,538. In this window the profit is 'alts rose from Sunday night to Monday night'; the BTC sign added nothing over simply being long, and the short half lost money.
cross_weekend_follow_alts.luck: The audit's cluster-bootstrap p-value is 0.131 and it does not survive the Holm correction; my weekend-clustered bootstrap reproduces 0.131, with a 5%-95% range for the total of -$372 to +$2,161. On its own that is about a 1-in-8 chance of seeing this from a strategy with no edge, before any allowance for selection. With 15 ideas audited (32 drafted), roughly two results this good are expected from pure noise, and 4 passed the gates. Sub-samples: without XRP p = 0.42; trades at or above the spec's default 0.5% threshold p = 0.35; shorts alone p = 0.60; only the long side looks significant (p = 0.025), and that is the always-long drift above. What the evidence shows: correct code, no look-ahead, realistic costs, a positive result in the unseen window. What it does not show: that the average trade is positive beyond chance, that the BTC weekend sign has predictive value, or that the result is spread across coins, quarters or signal strengths. The sister strategy with the same signal on BTC and ETH lost 2.0% in the same window and failed four gates.
strongest_evidence_against: The profit runs opposite to the stated cause. By size of BTC's weekend move: under 0.5%: 20 trades +$594 (avg +0.59R); 0.5-1%: 19 trades +$172; 1-2%: 50 trades +$565; over 2%: 40 trades on 14 weekends -$469 (avg -0.23R, 11 stopped out, shorts -$518). 69% of the profit comes from 10 weekends where BTC had barely moved, and on 3 of those the BTC sign differs one hour earlier or later. The second-best weekend (+$277) was triggered by a BTC move of -0.09%.
One coin: XRP is $743 of $862. Without it +1.2%, bootstrap p = 0.42.
A handful of weekends: the best 3 of 52 exceed the whole profit (-$18 without them); without the best 5, -$330. Two quarters carry 98%.
Not statistically distinguishable from luck: p = 0.131, fails Holm across 15 audited ideas; 10.3% of random-hour same-exposure draws do as well; 20.8% of other hour-of-week slots do as well.

Fragile to the signal hour: moving the Sunday 21:00 signal by one to five hours gives $492, $81, $196, $392 before and $69, $1, -$689, -$82, $20 after, against $862. The spec hour is the best of ten adjacent hours.

The BTC direction signal added nothing over being long: always long in the same top-3 alts on the same Sundays made $872 against the strategy's $766 (simulator figures); the strategy's shorts lost $123 at a 41% win rate.

The spec's own default parameters made +2.3% in validation, with shorts at -$438. Across the grid, the nine thr=0 cells made +5.4% to +15.8%, the nine thr=0.5% cells +0.2% to +3.0%, and the nine thr=1% cells -1.8% to +0.4%. Performance worsens as the signal is required to be stronger.
The same signal on BTC and ETH (cross_weekend_follow_majors) lost 2.0% in the same window and failed four gates.
strongest_evidence_for: Implementation is exact: 0 signal differences against an independent re-implementation in all 27 cells; the audited trades reproduce to the cent.
No look-ahead: 918 truncation probes over three seeds with 0 mismatches, and the universe lists verified as ranked on the prior 30 days for 38 months.

Execution is realistic: +8.53% with actual order-book costs, +8.57% one bar late with actual costs, +6.95% with fees doubled on top; positions are small against $10k depth and peak gross is 0.73x equity.
Positive in both the design window (+17.3%, 193 trades) and the unseen window, with a contained drawdown (-4.9%) while the top-10 basket fell 62%.
Weekend-signal slots as a group did better than weekday slots in validation (mean $462 against -$88), and the real direction beats a coin-flip direction in 94% of draws.
caveats_for_owner: My refutation is of the evidence, not the code. Nothing is broken; the result is simply too thin and too concentrated to trust with money. If the sealed test goes ahead anyway, a positive six months would still be mostly an XRP and long-side result unless the breakdown there looks different.

If it is paper traded regardless, do it as a watch-list item, not as champion. Things to watch: profit excluding XRP, profit on shorts, and profit on weekends where BTC moved more than 2% (the case the idea is supposed to be about). All three were flat or negative in validation.

It is one bet per week, up to three coins at once, all entered in the same hour and highly correlated: a wrong weekend costs up to about 1.5% of the account from this strategy alone (the worst weekend was -$158).

On Coinbase the contracts are whole units: 500 XRP, 5 SOL, 5,000 DOGE. A $50-risk position is often about one contract, so real risk per trade would range from $34 to $94 when rounding to nearest, with 13 of 127 trades skipped; or up to $293 on one trade if at least one contract is always taken. The backtest's fractional sizing cannot be replicated on a $10,000 account.

Costs and funding were modelled on Kraken; Coinbase's fees, funding and order books differ and were not tested. The Coinbase-subset audit uses today's listing applied to history, which is a forward-looking filter.

Disclosure: to get Coinbase contract sizes I fetched Coinbase's public product list once. The response also showed today's prices for these coins, which is information from after the validation window. I used only the contract sizes; no dataset bar from 2026-05-18 onward was loaded, and none of the findings above depend on it. The scratch copy was deleted.
The fourth leak-test seed (2026) had not finished when I reported; its output will be in /home/user/TRAYDINGCc/research/verify/cross_weekend_follow_alts/v2_leak.out.

My random-exposure nulls use a simplified simulator with no Guardian and no fold-boundary closes; it matches the engine exactly on 127 of 129 trades ($766 against the engine's $788 for those trades), so percentile figures are quoted against $766, not $862.

trend_quiet_grind.one_line: No bug, no look-ahead and realistic costs, but the +10.4% cannot be told apart from luck (p = 0.27): it comes from two rallies (Apr-May and Jul 2025), vanishes if 3 of the 135 trades are removed, and the strategy has lost money since August 2025, so it should not be relied on as champion.
implementation_differences: Entry signal: my independent plain-loop re-implementation from the spec text matched the module on 6,643,440 rows (40 symbols x 6 grid cells) except 1 row in PF_SUIUSD in the two q=0.7 cells, where the rank equals 0.7 to within floating-point rounding. No validation trade came from that row. Stops matched on every signal row.

All 135 validation trades re-checked against raw bars: signal present the bar before, coin in that month's universe, entry price, stop level, stop/time exit timing and price, fees and position size all agree. The single funding mismatch (2 cents, the trade closed at a quarter end) was my check's window, not the engine.

Not in the spec's exit text: the desk-wide Guardian closed 42 of the 135 trades (31%) on 9 halt days, for -$651. The spec lists only the 168-bar time stop and the protective stop. With the Guardian off the return is +7.4%; halting after 2 losses gives +17.2%, after 4 gives +9.1%.

The backtest lifts a Guardian halt automatically at the next UTC midnight. The live/paper engine (halt_sticky=True) stays halted until a human resumes it, so paper results will differ from the backtest unless the owner resumes promptly after each of roughly 9 halts per 17 months.

The parameters actually traded in validation were never the Hunter's defaults (q 0.8, stop 5 ATR). Walk-forward chose stop 7 ATR in all six quarters, with q 0.7 for the first two and q 0.9 for the last four. This is allowed by the protocol, but the default cell on its own made -0.03% with a -21.8% drawdown in validation (design: +22.6%).
trend_quiet_grind.lookahead_detail: None found. Every input (close, high, low) is from bar t or earlier: the efficiency ratio, the 4,320-bar rolling rank and the ATR are all trailing, and there is no shift(-n) or whole-sample statistic. harness.leak_test passed with seeds 1, 7 and 42 (119 probes each across all 6 cells, 0 mismatches), on top of the audit's own 349 probes and 191-probe trade replay. The universe is used correctly: every trade's coin was in the month's top-10 at both signal and entry, and for 5 months I recomputed the top-10 from daily volume of the prior 30 days and it matched the list exactly (an in-month ranking would overlap only 8-9 of 10). Entries do fill at the signal bar's close (open[t+1] equals close[t] on all 135 trades), but that price is not needed: one bar late gives +10.3%.
trend_quiet_grind.real_cost_check: Costs are not the weakness. At the 135 entry bars the modelled half-spread averages 3.26 bps, against an actual 3.58 bps in the signal bar and 3.53 bps in the fill bar (actual/modelled 1.11 and 1.05; worst single entry 16.2 bps actual vs 11.9 modelled). On stop exits the model charges 6.33 bps against an actual 3.5-3.7 bps, so it is conservative there. Total modelled slippage is $54; actual is $49 (fill/exit bar) to $66 (worse of two adjacent bars, doubled on stops). Full engine re-runs with the actual order-book half-spread: +10.34% (same bar) and +10.25% (worse of two bars). One bar late AND actual costs: +10.18% to +10.26%. Actual worse-of-two slippage plus fees doubled, funding doubled and one bar late: +8.33%. Funding is the least certain cost: 81% of position-hours use estimated funding; only $49 was paid, and at 5x that the return is still +8.45%. Positions are small (median notional $594, range $210-$2,828; no trade hit the 1x cap), 32% of trades share an entry hour with another coin (at most 4 in one hour), there were at most 9 simultaneous positions and peak gross exposure was $10,072 (1.01x equity). Coinbase whole contracts: a 0.01 BTC contract was worth $754-$1,240 at validation prices, so the 15 BTC trades wanted 0.65-2.59 contracts; nearest-contract rounding moves risk per trade to $34-$77 instead of $50, and rounding down drops 3 of the 15 trades (BTC profit $247 becomes $311 or $146). ETH (0.1 ETH, $175-$374) wanted 1.8-5.5 contracts, with risk $40-$57. Other coins' contract sizes are not in the repo.
trend_quiet_grind.concentration: Extremely concentrated in time. The 135 trades fall into 12 episodes (entries less than 7 days apart); 4 were profitable. Two of them (20 Apr-28 May 2025, +$1,092; 6-31 Jul 2025, +$1,306) made +$2,398 against a total of +$1,039; the other ten lost -$1,359. By quarter: -6.6%, +10.9%, +10.9%, -0.4%, -4.5%, +0.2%. Without the best quarter the return is -0.5%; without the best two, -11.4%. Without the best month it is -2.7%; without the best two, -12.5%. Without the best 5 of 54 exit days it is -19.6%. Without the best 3 trades (2% of trades) it is -$25; without the best 10, -$1,402. 15 trades with R above 2 made $3,026; win rate is 37% and the median trade is -0.37R. By symbol: 9 of 18 profitable; ETH alone made $669 of $1,039. Without ETH the return is +3.7% (engine re-run +3.4%, p = 0.43); without ETH and SUI, -0.2%; without the top three, -2.7%. All trades are long. Coinbase-listed coins only: +13.4% with the same parameters, +12.0% when the walk-forward is re-fitted (136 trades, p = 0.26, all gates pass, but one bar late falls to +7.1%); the 17 non-Coinbase trades lost -$205. Every fixed grid cell shows the same dependence: each is -10% to -17% without its best two months.
trend_quiet_grind.exposure_check: Mixed: it beats blind long exposure, but not clearly anything smarter than plain momentum. All nulls ran through the same engine, folds, 7-ATR stop, 168-bar hold, Guardian and costs, 300 draws each. (B) Random universe coin, random month, random hour, same trade count: mean -6.3%, 5th-95th percentile -15.0% to +2.8%; the real +10.4% beats 99.3% of draws. Always-long every universe coin lost -35.8%. So the rule did pick better coin-months than chance in a window where the basket fell 62%. (C) Random hours in the same coin-quarters when the 14-day return is positive (momentum without the smoothness filter): mean +1.4%, 95th percentile +12.2%; real beats 90% (p about 0.10, not significant). The deterministic versions agree: 14-day return > 0 with no filter +5.1% (drawdown -32%), choppy rises +1.5%, smooth falls bought -4.9%. (A) Random hours in the same coin-months as the real trades: mean +11.4%, and 53% of draws do as well or better. This null is somewhat generous because it includes hours before the signal, but it shows the exact entry hour carries no value; the result is which coins in which months. Shifting the whole signal stream by 3, 6, 12, 24 or 48 hours gives +14.8%, +23.8%, +17.4%, +14.0% and +5.0%, so the result moves by more than its own size on arbitrary timing changes. Delaying each real entry by a random 1-72 h gives a mean of +4.4% (real beats 92%). I discarded a +/-3.5-day null (mean +27%) because entering before a known future signal is itself look-ahead.
trend_quiet_grind.luck: The evidence does not show an edge. The audit's cluster-bootstrap p-value is 0.271 (0.267 by exit day, 0.272 by exit week); resampling at the level the profit actually clusters gives 0.30 by month and 0.31 by episode (12 episodes, mean +$87, sd $547, t = 0.55). The per-trade t-statistic is 1.07 even ignoring clustering. It fails Holm, which would need roughly p < 0.003 across 15 audits. Across the 15 audited strategies, 4 have p <= 0.271, and pure chance predicts 4.1 of 15, so the leaderboard as a whole looks like what no-edge strategies produce; this one is the fourth of those four. A further 17 drafted ideas were never audited. The Hunter's own default setting, which made +22.6% in design, made -0.03% in validation. The walk-forward's +10.4% sits near the top of the fixed-cell range (-0.03% to +11.7%, median +7.6%). What the evidence does show: the code is right, costs are realistic, and the rule lost less than holding. Beating a basket that fell 62% is a low bar for a strategy that is flat 67% of the time.
strongest_evidence_against: Luck cannot be excluded: p = 0.271 (0.31 when resampling the 12 episodes), no Holm survival, and 4 of 15 audited strategies reach p <= 0.271 where chance alone predicts 4.1.

Two rallies carry everything: Apr-May 2025 and Jul 2025 made +$2,398; the other ten episodes lost -$1,359. Without the best quarter the return is -0.5%, without the best 3 trades of 135 it is -$25, and without the best 5 exit days it is -19.6%.
It has been losing going into the sealed period: trades exiting from 1 Aug 2025 onward total -$700 (43 trades, 21% winners), and the last three quarters are -0.4%, -4.5% and +0.2%.

The Hunter's own 'fading' alarm is already on at the end of validation: the last 30 trades won 20% (alarm level 35%, design 44%) for -$440, and the Dec 2025-Jan 2026 episode was 17 trades in 10 coins that lost -$488 together.

The strategy as the Hunter specified it (q 0.8, stop 5 ATR) did not replicate: +22.6% in design, -0.03% in validation with a -21.8% drawdown and a 13-trade losing streak. The pass rests on the 7-ATR cells the walk-forward picked.
Random entry hours in the same coin-months do as well or better 53% of the time, and against plain 14-day momentum exposure the smoothness filter is not significant (p about 0.10).
The result swings by more than its own size on arbitrary changes: shifting signals 3-48 hours gives +5.0% to +23.8%, and the Coinbase re-fit drops from +12.0% to +7.1% when one bar late.
Single-coin dependence: without ETH the return is +3.4% (p = 0.43); without ETH and SUI it is -0.2%.
strongest_evidence_for: Implementation is faithful: independent re-implementation matches on 6.6 million rows, and all 135 trades reconcile against raw bars.
No look-ahead: 3 extra leak-test seeds (357 probes) plus the audit's 349 probes and 191-probe trade replay all clean; universe ranking confirmed to use the prior 30 days.

Costs are realistic and the result is insensitive to them: +10.25% with actual order-book costs, +10.18% when also one bar late, +8.33% with actual slippage, doubled fees, doubled funding and one bar late.
It beats blind long exposure: real result is above 99.3% of 300 random coin-month long draws (mean -6.3%), while always-long lost -35.8%.
Coinbase-listed coins only still pass every gate (+12.0% re-fitted, 136 trades), and BTC and ETH alone made +9.1% (27 trades, p = 0.08).
5 of 6 grid cells were profitable in validation (median +7.6%), and the walk-forward over all 11 quarters since Oct 2023 made +44.0%, though 5 of those quarters are inside the Hunter's design window.
caveats_for_owner: My refutation is statistical, not a bug: the code does what the rules say and the costs are fair. The problem is that +10.4% over 17 months is the kind of number chance produces about one time in four, and this desk tested 15 strategies.

This is a long-only momentum rule that makes money only in a few broad rallies. Expect long stretches of small losses (63% of trades lose; 10 of 12 trade clusters lost or barely broke even) while waiting for a rally that may not come.
It was losing at the end of the test window (-$700 since August 2025) and its own designer's warning sign (win rate under 35% over the last 30 trades) is already triggered at 20%.

If it is paper traded anyway, do not treat a profitable six months as proof: one rally decides the outcome. Judge it on whether it loses small outside rallies, and stop if a cluster of 3 or more coins stops out together again.

The backtest's safety halt resets itself at midnight UTC; the live bot stays halted until you resume it. There were about 9 halts in 17 months, and the halt behaviour changes the result (Guardian off: +7.4%).

On Coinbase, whole-contract sizing matters for BTC: a $50-risk position wanted 0.65-2.59 contracts, so real risk per BTC trade would be $34-$77, or the trade is skipped. Contract sizes for other coins were not checked, and the Coinbase coin list is today's list applied to the past.

81% of position-hours used estimated rather than published funding. The amount is small ($49) and 5x that still leaves +8.45%, but Coinbase's funding and fees differ from Kraken's and were not modelled.
The account in the backtest does not compound and cannot go broke; drawdown reached -12.2% in the walk-forward and -17% to -22% in neighbouring fixed settings.
